extracted.intended_audience: poets, playwrights, and moral essayists (readers/writers of The Spectator interested in comedy, character-drawing, and public manners)
extracted.subtask_description: Advice and standards for composing comic plays/essays: how to draw characters, direct laughter, and use moralizing devices (allegory, satire, fable) to reform manners without coarse language. Focuses on characterization, dialogue, and the ethical aim of humour.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poets should attempt honesty which becomes their characters
rubrics_metrics.description: There is room enough to catch at Men's Hearts to their Good and Advantage, if the Poets will attempt it with the Honesty which becomes their Characters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Portray characters honestly and consistently so that their representation can reform or 'smite and reprove' the audience's vices; the poet's moral purpose should align with the character's nature rather than using characters merely for spectacle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Depict virtue joined with wit and humour
rubrics_metrics.description: A Man that is Temperate, Generous, Valiant, Chaste, Faithful and Honest, may, at the same time, have Wit, Humour, Mirth, Good-breeding, and Gallantry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Show virtuous characters as lively and entertaining rather than dull moral exemplars: invent occasions to display their noble virtues alongside wit so they appeal to the audience and model better conduct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid the customary spurious force of oaths and feeble dialogue
rubrics_metrics.description: Steele's Plays were as pure as his 'Spectator' Essays, absolutely discarding the customary way of enforcing feeble dialogues by the spurious force of oaths, and aiming at a wholesome influence upon his audience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reject coarse, oath-filled dialogue used as a cheap substitute for forceful writing; prefer clean, morally edifying speech that exerts genuine influence on the audience's sentiments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use a character's unmasking at the catastrophe for moral effect
rubrics_metrics.description: Might not such a one divert the Audience quite as well, if at the Catastrophe he were found out for a Traitor, and met with Contempt accordingly?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recast or reveal characters at the conclusion (catastrophe) so that villainy is exposed and treated with contempt, producing moral satisfaction and reinforcing the play's corrective aims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Direct laughter at folly of characters, not at the author or superior person
rubrics_metrics.description: When you did me the Honour to be so merry over my Paper, you laughed at the Idiot, the German Courtier, the Gaper, the Merry-Andrew, the Haberdasher, the Biter, the Butt, and not at [the author].
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good comedy causes the audience to laugh at clearly ridiculous social types (the fool, the gawper, the mountebank) rather than aiming mockery at the writer or at properly placed virtue; laughter should target folly to instruct rather than to demean indiscriminately.

rubrics_metrics.name: Depict a single 'darling vice' to enable moral correction
rubrics_metrics.description: There is seldom a Person devoted to above one Darling Vice at a time, so that there is room enough to catch at Men's Hearts to their Good and Advantage...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Concentrate a character's failings around a dominant vice (avarice, luxury, intemperance, etc.) so satire and comic exposure can focus and be effective in reforming that fault.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use allegory and personification to illustrate moral principles
rubrics_metrics.description: I threw my Thoughts into a little kind of Allegory or Fable... There were two very powerful Tyrants engaged in a perpetual War against each other: The Name of the first was Luxury, and of the second Avarice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ fable/personified characters (Luxury, Avarice, Poverty, Plenty) to dramatize abstract moral conflicts; allegory makes complex civic or ethical points concrete and memorable for readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Employ historical analogy to generalize social observations
rubrics_metrics.description: When a Government flourishes in Conquests, and is secure from foreign Attacks, it naturally falls into all the Pleasures of Luxury... The most Elegant and Correct of all the Latin Historians observes...the Republick sunk into those two Vices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Support moral claims by alluding to historical examples (e.g., Rome's descent into luxury and avarice) to lend weight and generality to the satiric lesson.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use satire and social complaint to reform everyday manners
rubrics_metrics.description: Take these mischievous People, the Peepers, into your Consideration: I doubt not but you will think a Peeper as much more pernicious than a Starer...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Target commonplace breaches of decorum (peepers, starers, improper conduct at divine service) in satirical letters or sketches to prompt readers to self-correction of manners.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character-types should be recognizable and observed from life
rubrics_metrics.description: I have with great Pains and Industry made my Observations from time to time upon these Sages... The elder Proficients employ themselves in inspecting mores hominum multorum... Our younger Students are content to carry their Speculations as yet no farther than Bowling-greens, Billiard-Tables, and such like Places.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Base comic portraits on careful observation of real social types (the idler, the 'Lownger', the fop) and their habitual practices; vivid, specific detail (coaches, diversions, habits) makes satire effective and recognizable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Promote reform by educating the admirer as well as the admired
rubrics_metrics.description: In order to embellish the Mistress, you should give a new Education to the Lover, and teach the Men not to be any longer dazzled by false Charms and unreal Beauty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When aiming at social improvement, target both the objects of desire and those who admire them: instructing admirers (e.g., teaching men to prize virtue over mere beauty) strengthens the essay's reforming purpose.
